name: Nora Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, forty-three, and I'm still the junior electrician even though some of the qualified people are younger than me. I got my vocational certificate last year after years of cleaning work, and now I help wire houses and repair shop circuits under a supervisor. I love seeing a room light up, but I still need someone beside me for the difficult tests.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Emil does billing work for a supplier, and we have an eight-year-old, a twelve-year-old and a mortgage. My pay is low, we've got about three weeks of expenses saved and there are only a few electrical firms nearby. I use AI every day to quiz myself on course notes and write practice fault descriptions, never as permission to touch a live circuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small useful tool is still useful, even if the big promises fade. I'd show my supervisor the practice questions I've made, but I wouldn't tell the apprentice next to me that a chat window is a teacher. We both need the person who checks our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already anxious about the mortgage, without needing AI to do anything dramatic. One unpaid week would eat a large part of our three-week cushion. I don't regret changing trades. Being forty-three doesn't make my beginner's wage bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised repair shifts now and during the first year, and spend fifteen minutes nightly checking AI practice questions against my course book. Emil and I would cancel the two takeaway meals we usually buy each month until we have breathing room. I'd use the saved money for the next mortgage payment rather than pretend it's spare cash for a new course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some pleasure left in the work. I can enjoy learning a new test in the morning and still count the days to payday at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if one of you missed a week's pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop any spending that could wait and ring the mortgage lender before missing a payment to ask what options actually exist. I don't know whether we'd qualify for help, which is why I wouldn't wait for the red letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you stop a wrong practice answer becoming a mistake on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write the answer from the course book beside it and ask my supervisor if the two don't match. The tool can help me form a question, but it doesn't sign off a wire.

say: I think **small useful tools** still help even when the largest promises fade.
I'd tell another junior that **AI practice** cannot replace the person checking our electrical work.
think: I'm already **anxious about the mortgage**, even without dramatic change from AI.
One unpaid week would consume much of our **three-week cushion** while I earn a beginner's wage.
do: Keep **supervised shifts** and check nightly AI practice against my vocational course book.
Cancel **two monthly takeaways** and put that money towards the next mortgage payment.
feel: **Anxious but engaged**, enjoying new skills while counting the days to payday.
S0.quote: Being forty-three doesn't make my beginner's wage bigger.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI practice** supports a junior learner, with the course book and supervisor retaining authority over what happens on site.
The **mortgage pressure** predates the scenario; cancelling takeaways funds a current bill rather than an invented reserve or course budget.

steps.text: Keep the supervised home and shop repair shifts
Cancel two monthly takeaways to help cover the next mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say try the new tools on real examples and tell us what hours the firm is changing. I'd help compare an AI parts list with the one my supervisor made, but I wouldn't pretend I can judge a whole installation yet. I want something that helps me learn, not something that lets the firm say learning is finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own shifts could shrink if the senior electrician can do the paperwork faster and no longer needs so much junior help between visits. Emil's billing work is also close to the checking and answering on that card. Neither of us has a spare wage to absorb the other's cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my supervisor for a weekly twenty-minute paid session checking AI practice lists against finished jobs. In the first year I'd record which paid tasks I can do safely and ask the owner directly how junior hours will be set. At home we'd keep the takeaway cut and postpone replacing our working television until we know what happens to both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and impatient to get better. I like the tools, but I don't like wondering whether being quicker means I'm needed for fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the paid session teach that you cannot get from the tool alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why the supervisor rejected a cheap fitting or added time to a repair. I can memorise the neat list and still not understand the damp wall or the damaged cable behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Emil to check at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the new billing system changes staffing or just clears the late invoices. I'd rather we both ask a plain question now than tell each other everything is fine because nobody has said otherwise.

say: I'd ask firms to state **changed hours** while testing tools on real examples.
I'd say **faster learning** does not mean a junior can safely judge an entire installation.
think: My **junior shifts could shrink** if quicker paperwork reduces the help a senior electrician needs.
Emil's **billing work** is also exposed, and neither household wage can easily absorb the other's cut.
do: Request **twenty paid minutes** weekly to compare AI practice lists with a supervisor's finished jobs.
Record **safe paid tasks** and ask the owner how junior hours will be set in the first year.
Keep the **takeaway cut** and postpone replacing the working television while checking both wages.
feel: **Anxious and impatient**, wanting to improve without losing the paid hours needed to learn.
S1.quote: I like the tools, but I don't like wondering whether being quicker means I'm needed for fewer hours.
fieldNote: She **welcomes tools** without overstating her junior competence, asking a supervisor to explain decisions that a parts list hides.
Both **household earners** could face reduced hours, making spending restraint concrete rather than a generic response to distant technology.

steps.text: Request weekly paid supervision to compare AI lists with finished repairs
Keep takeaway cuts and delay replacing the working television

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years isn't much warning for families paying for the present month. Planning changes in 2028, but that doesn't mean I can do the physical work alone; I still need a supervisor. I'd ask employers for honest written hours rather than another cheerful message about opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Emil to lose a large part of the billing income when almost all thinking work becomes cheaper in 2028. My hands-on work may continue until robots catch up around 2031, but my low wage cannot carry the mortgage and both children alone. I would be awake wondering how many payments the savings could cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd sit down with Emil and write a budget using only my current wage, then contact the lender to ask about hardship options and their conditions. I'd cancel our planned weekend away before its final payment is due. In the first year after 2028, if Emil's income falls, we'd apply for any support we're actually eligible for; I'd also apply to advertised supervised electrical posts only if wages and travel leave us better off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even though I'm already reaching for a pen. A budget can show me the hole without giving me the money to fill it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the cancelled weekend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're keeping money for the house and everyday things, and we'll do a picnic instead. I wouldn't tell them the house is definitely safe, because I don't know, but they don't need every frightened thought I have at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which lender answer would you need in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How long any lower payment lasts, what gets added to the debt and whether the interest keeps growing. I'd ask for the total cost before agreeing; a smaller number this month can hide a bigger problem later.

say: I'd ask for **honest written hours** because two years gives mortgage-paying families little room.
I'd say **thinking AI first** does not make a junior suddenly able to work without supervision.
think: I expect a **large billing-income loss** for Emil when thinking work becomes cheaper in 2028.
My **low hands-on wage** cannot carry the mortgage and children alone while we wait for robots around 2031.
do: Write a **single-wage budget** now and ask the lender about hardship terms and total costs.
Cancel the **weekend away** before its final payment is due.
Apply after income falls for **eligible support** and affordable posted electrical work that still provides supervision.
feel: **Alarmed**, expecting a major household income loss that the current savings cannot cover for long.
S2.quote: A budget can show me the hole without giving me the money to fill it.
fieldNote: The **household exposure** arrives through billing in 2028, before physical robots, so she does not mistake hands-on delay for mortgage security.
Her **support request** depends on eligibility and written lender costs; another electrical post must be advertised, supervised and financially worthwhile.

steps.text: Ask the mortgage lender about hardship terms and total borrowing costs
Apply for eligible support if billing income falls after 2028
Cancel the weekend away before its final payment
Apply for posted supervised electrical jobs only where travel and wages improve finances

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a family a chance to get past the next bill before making every choice. I'd ask both employers to put paid training options on paper. I don't care whether the answer comes from a firm or a public scheme, as long as the place and the paid time actually exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both our incomes could shrink, but I have longer to become useful at the physical work before planning changes in 2031. The robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, not ready to stop earning. Emil would have longer to compare real work options too, though no course promises safety from this whole picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask now for a paid place on the next supervised fault-testing class, enrolling only if the employer pays the fee and keeps my usual wage during class. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep checking new planning tools against supervised site work, rather than use them to skip practical checks. Emil and I would review the budget every three months and save forty a month only when all bills are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not staring at an immediate cliff. I can picture a sequence of paid lessons and bills paid on time, even if I can't promise the sequence lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why forty a month rather than a bigger target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we're starting with three weeks saved, two children and a mortgage, not an empty sheet of paper. Forty is something we might manage after the takeaway cut; if a school expense uses it, the saving waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the class is free but during unpaid work time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't enrol on those terms. I need the practice, but I also need the wage that pays for my children's dinner that week.

say: I'd ask both employers for **written paid-training options** while there is time to compare them.
I care about real places and **paid time**, whether the route comes from a firm or public scheme.
think: Both **household incomes could shrink**, but five years gives me longer to build practical competence before 2031.
At **fifty-one in 2034**, I'll still need income when robots reach hands-on work.
do: Enrol in **supervised fault testing** only with employer-paid fees and usual wages maintained during class.
Check **new planning tools** against supervised site work in the first year after 2031.
Review the **household budget** quarterly and save forty monthly only after covering all bills.
feel: **Anxious but less cornered**, able to imagine paid lessons alongside ordinary bills.
S3.quote: I need the practice, but I also need the wage that pays for my children's dinner that week.
fieldNote: Her **training condition** explicitly covers both tuition and lost wages, avoiding a plan that thin savings could not support.
The **forty-monthly target** is conditional on real household costs, while a longer warning improves options without guaranteeing future employment.

steps.text: Enrol in supervised fault testing only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages
Check planning tools against supervised site work after 2031
Save forty monthly only after household bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us a chance to plan the children's studies without pretending we know the perfect safe job. I'd want them to learn a mix of things and see real work, not be sent towards my trade just because I can hold a screwdriver. I'd still ask for paid learning for adults who already have bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our money is tight now even if the big change waits until 2036. The children will be eighteen and twenty-two by then, and I will be fifty-three; robots follow around 2039, when I'll be fifty-six. Some costs may change, but I can't assume the mortgage is gone or the children need no help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pursue the same funded testing class now and keep the forty-a-month saving target only when bills permit. This year I'd ask the children's school about free work visits across several fields, without choosing a career for them. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare posted paid service jobs if our hours fall, checking wages, travel and supervision before changing employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the present budget, but less trapped by the future. Ten years gives us time to change the plan more than once, which feels useful when you're raising children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if one child wanted to be an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help arrange a safe work visit and explain both the good parts and the uncertain ones. I wouldn't promise a job for life or tell the child to give up an interest because of one picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reduce the saving target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mortgage increase, a school trip we agree to pay for, or a necessary repair. I want a cushion. Writing a savings target in a notebook doesn't make the other costs vanish.

say: I'd give the children **varied work visits** rather than pretend there is one perfect safe career.
I'd keep asking for **paid adult learning** because existing household bills do not disappear during training.
think: Our **budget is tight now**, even if thinking AI waits until 2036 and robots until around 2039.
I cannot assume the **mortgage and children** stop needing money when they are older and I'm still working age.
do: Pursue **fault testing** only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages, saving forty monthly when bills permit.
Ask the school this year about **free work visits** across several fields.
Compare **posted service jobs** after 2036 if hours fall, checking wages, travel and supervision.
feel: **Anxious about today**, but less trapped by the future when family plans can be revised.
S4.quote: Writing a savings target in a notebook doesn't make the other costs vanish.
fieldNote: Her **children's ages** change with the scenario dates, but she does not assume independent adulthood removes every family expense or the mortgage.
She **broadens school exposure** without choosing a supposedly safe occupation, while keeping saving and training tied to actual household affordability.

steps.text: Take supervised fault testing only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages
Save forty monthly when household bills permit
Ask the school about free work visits across several fields
Compare posted service jobs after 2036 if hours fall, checking wages, travel and supervision

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Emil's billing wage could go before my junior wage can carry the household. Paid supervised training with my wage kept would help, and clear temporary support if our income falls. I need somebody to state the conditions before I build a budget around help we might never receive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the older beginner how many people depend on the beginner's wage. I'm learning beside people with a very different monthly bill, even when we're holding the same screwdriver. I want to get good at this without making my children pay for every lesson.

headlineQuote: Ask the older beginner how many people depend on the beginner's wage.
portrait: Nora is a **43-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, still learning under supervision after changing from cleaning work.
She has **three weeks saved**, low pay, few local employers, two schoolchildren and a mortgage with partner Emil.
Her **daily AI practice** helps her ask questions, while supervisors and course books remain the authority on safe electrical work.
She is **already anxious** about bills; rapid AGI alarms her because Emil's billing income could disappear before her wage supports the household.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens Emil's billing wage before her junior earnings can support their mortgage and children.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid supervised training** must cover both fees and her usual wages.
Any **temporary income support** needs clear eligibility and conditions before she budgets around it.
